In statistics, '''modes of variation'''<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Castro|first1=P. E.|last2=Lawton|first2=W. H.|last3=Sylvestre|first3=E. A.|date=November 1986|title=Principal Modes of Variation for Processes with Continuous Sample Curves|journal=Technometrics|volume=28|issue=4|pages=329|doi=10.2307/1268982|jstor=1268982|issn=0040-1706}}</ref> are a continuously indexed set of vectors or functions that are centered at a mean and are used to depict the variation in a population or sample. Typically, variation patterns in the data can be decomposed in descending order of [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] with the directions represented by the corresponding [[eigenbasis|eigenvectors]] or [[Eigenfunction|eigenfunctions]]. Modes of variation provide a visualization of this decomposition and an efficient description of variation around the mean. Both in [[principal component analysis]] (PCA) and in [[functional principal component analysis]] (FPCA), modes of variation play an important role in visualizing and describing the variation in the data contributed by each eigencomponent.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Jane-Ling|last2=Chiou|first2=Jeng-Min|last3=Müller|first3=Hans-Georg|date=June 2016|title=Functional Data Analysis|journal=[[Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application]]|volume=3|issue=1|pages=257–295|doi=10.1146/annurev-statistics-041715-033624|issn=2326-8298|url=https://zenodo.org/record/895750|doi-access=free}}</ref> In real-world applications, the eigencomponents and associated modes of variation aid to interpret complex data, especially in [[exploratory data analysis]] (EDA).

== Formulation ==
Modes of variation are a natural extension of [[Principal component analysis|PCA]] and [[Functional principal component analysis|FPCA]]. 

=== Modes of variation in [[Principal component analysis|PCA]] ===
If a random vector <math>\mathbf{X}=(X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_p)^T</math> has the mean vector <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}_p</math>, and the covariance matrix <math>\mathbf{\Sigma}_{p\times p}</math> with [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] <math>\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \cdots \geq \lambda_p\geq0</math> and corresponding [[Orthonormality|orthonormal]] [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvectors]] <math>\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \cdots,\mathbf{e}_p</math>, by [[Eigendecomposition of a matrix|eigendecomposition of a real symmetric matrix]], the covariance matrix <math>\mathbf{\Sigma}</math> can be decomposed as
:<math>\mathbf{\Sigma}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T,</math>
where <math>\mathbf{Q}</math> is an [[orthogonal matrix]] whose columns are the eigenvectors of <math>\mathbf{\Sigma}</math>, and <math>\mathbf{\Lambda}</math> is a [[diagonal matrix]] whose entries are the eigenvalues of <math>\mathbf{\Sigma}</math>. By the [[Karhunen–Loève theorem|Karhunen–Loève expansion]] for random vectors, one can express the centered [[Multivariate random variable|random vector]] in the eigenbasis 
:<math>\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu}=\sum_{k=1}^p\xi_k\mathbf{e}_k,</math>

where <math>\xi_k=\mathbf{e}_k^T(\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu})</math> is the principal component<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kleffe |first=Jürgen |date=January 1973 |title=Principal components of random variables with values in a seperable {{sic|hide=y}} HILBERT space |journal=Mathematische Operationsforschung und Statistik |volume=4 |issue=5 |pages=391–406 |doi=10.1080/02331887308801137 |issn=0047-6277}}</ref> associated with the <math> k</math>-th eigenvector <math>\mathbf{e}_k</math>, with the properties
:<math>\operatorname{E}(\xi_k)=0, \operatorname{Var}(\xi_k)=\lambda_k,</math> and <math>\operatorname{E}(\xi_k\xi_l)=0\ \text{for}\ l\neq k.</math>

Then the <math>k</math>-th mode of variation of <math>\mathbf{X}</math> is the set of vectors, indexed by <math>\alpha</math>, 

:<math>\mathbf{m}_{k, \alpha}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\pm \alpha\sqrt{\lambda_k}\mathbf{e}_k, \alpha\in[-A, A],</math>

where <math>A</math> is typically selected as <math>2\ \text{or}\ 3</math>.

=== Modes of variation in [[Functional principal component analysis|FPCA]] ===
For a [[Square-integrable function|square-integrable]] [[random function]] <math>X(t), t \in \mathcal{T}\subset R^p</math>, where typically <math>p=1</math> and <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is an interval, denote the mean function by <math> \mu(t) = \operatorname{E}(X(t)) </math>, and the [[covariance function]] by 

:<math> G(s, t) = \operatorname{Cov}(X(s), X(t)) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \lambda_k \varphi_k(s) \varphi_k(t), </math>

where <math>\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \cdots \geq 0</math> are the eigenvalues and <math>\{\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \cdots\}</math> are the [[orthonormality|orthonormal]] eigenfunctions of the linear [[Hilbert–Schmidt operator]]
:<math> G: L^2(\mathcal{T}) \rightarrow L^2(\mathcal{T}),\, G(f) = \int_\mathcal{T} G(s, t) f(s) ds. </math>

By the [[Karhunen–Loève theorem]], one can express the centered function in the eigenbasis, 

:<math> X(t) - \mu(t) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \xi_k \varphi_k(t),
</math>
where 
:<math> \xi_k = \int_\mathcal{T} (X(t) - \mu(t)) \varphi_k(t) dt 
</math>

is the <math>k</math>-th principal component with the properties
:<math> \operatorname{E}(\xi_k) = 0, \operatorname{Var}(\xi_k) = \lambda_k,</math> and <math>\operatorname{E}(\xi_k \xi_l) = 0 \text{ for } l \ne k.</math>

Then the <math>k</math>-th mode of variation of <math>X(t)</math> is the set of functions, indexed by <math>\alpha</math>,

:<math>m_{k, \alpha}(t)=\mu(t)\pm \alpha\sqrt{\lambda_k}\varphi_k(t),\ t\in \mathcal{T},\ \alpha\in [-A, A]</math>

that are viewed simultaneously over the range of <math>\alpha</math>, usually for <math>A=2\ \text{or}\ 3</math>.<ref name=":0" />

== Estimation ==
The formulation above is derived from properties of the population. Estimation is needed in real-world applications. The key idea is to estimate mean and covariance.

=== Modes of variation in [[Principal component analysis|PCA]] ===
Suppose the data <math>\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \cdots, \mathbf{x}_n</math> represent <math>n</math> independent drawings from some <math>p</math>-dimensional population <math>\mathbf{X}</math> with mean vector <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> and covariance matrix <math>\mathbf{\Sigma}</math>. These data yield the sample mean vector <math>\overline\mathbf{{x}}</math>, and the sample covariance matrix <math>\mathbf{S}</math> with eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs <math>(\hat{\lambda}_1, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1), (\hat{\lambda}_2, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2), \cdots, (\hat{\lambda}_p, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_p)</math>. Then the <math>k</math>-th mode of variation of <math>\mathbf{X}</math> can be estimated by

: <math>\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{k, \alpha}=\overline{\mathbf{x}}\pm \alpha\sqrt{\hat{\lambda}_k}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_k, \alpha\in [-A, A].</math>

=== Modes of variation in [[Functional principal component analysis|FPCA]] ===
Consider <math>n</math> realizations <math>X_1(t), X_2(t), \cdots, X_n(t)</math> of a [[Square-integrable function|square-integrable]] [[stochastic process|random function]] <math>X(t), t \in \mathcal{T}</math> with the mean function <math> \mu(t) = \operatorname{E}(X(t)) </math> and the covariance function <math> G(s, t) = \operatorname{Cov}(X(s), X(t)) </math>. [[Functional principal component analysis]] provides methods for the estimation of <math> \mu(t) </math> and <math> G(s, t) </math> in detail, often involving point wise estimate and [[interpolation]]. Substituting estimates for the unknown quantities, the <math>k</math>-th mode of variation of <math>X(t)</math> can be estimated by

: <math>\hat{m}_{k, \alpha}(t)=\hat{\mu}(t)\pm \alpha\sqrt{\hat{\lambda}_k}\hat{\varphi}_k(t), t\in \mathcal{T}, \alpha\in [-A, A].</math>

== Applications ==
[[File:Movfemale.svg|thumb|400px|The first and second modes of variation of female mortality data from 41 countries in 2003<ref name=":1" />]]
[[File:Movmale.svg|thumb|400px|The first and second modes of variation of male mortality data from 41 countries in 2003<ref name=":1" />]]
Modes of variation are useful to visualize and describe the variation patterns in the data sorted by the eigenvalues. In real-world applications, modes of variation associated with eigencomponents allow to interpret complex data, such as the evolution of function traits<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kirkpatrick|first1=Mark|last2=Heckman|first2=Nancy|date=August 1989|title=A quantitative genetic model for growth, shape, reaction norms, and other infinite-dimensional characters|journal=Journal of Mathematical Biology|volume=27|issue=4|pages=429–450|doi=10.1007/bf00290638|pmid=2769086|s2cid=46336613|issn=0303-6812}}</ref> and other infinite-dimensional data.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jones|first1=M. C.|last2=Rice|first2=John A.|date=May 1992|title=Displaying the Important Features of Large Collections of Similar Curves|journal=The American Statistician|volume=46|issue=2|pages=140–145|doi=10.1080/00031305.1992.10475870|issn=0003-1305}}</ref> To illustrate how modes of variation work in practice, two examples are shown in the graphs to the right, which display the first two modes of variation. The solid curve represents the sample mean function. The dashed, dot-dashed, and dotted curves correspond to modes of variation with <math>\alpha=\pm1, \pm2,</math> and <math>\pm3</math>, respectively.

The first graph displays the first two modes of variation of female mortality data from 41 countries in 2003.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mortality.org/|title=Human Mortality Database|website=www.mortality.org|access-date=2020-03-12}}</ref> The object of interest is log [[Failure rate|hazard function]] between ages 0 and 100 years. The first mode of variation suggests that the variation of female mortality is smaller for ages around 0 or 100, and larger for ages around 25. An appropriate and intuitive interpretation is that mortality around 25 is driven by accidental death, while around 0 or 100, mortality is related to congenital disease or natural death. 

Compared to female mortality data, modes of variation of male mortality data shows higher mortality after around age 20, possibly related to the fact that life expectancy for women is higher than that for men.
